title: How the Western Front Happened — Minute by Minute
hook: Christmas Eve 1914: the Germans shout Merry Christmas across no man's land, and a British captain writes that his men can't shoot them in cold blood. Five days later he is dead, and the war has 1,412 days left to run.
about: The Western Front of the First World War, 1914-1918, lived from both sides of the trenches: the march through Belgium, life two metres underground, the Christmas truce in the letters of Captain Robert Miles, Lieutenant Johannes Niemann, Kurt Zehmisch and Gervais Morillon, the first gas attack at Ypres, the painter Franz Marc at Verdun, seven thirty on the first day of the Somme, the mutinies of 1917, Germany's last gamble, and the last minutes of 11 November 1918.
talkNote: Dialogue scenes are dramatized; every fact comes from the sources below. Lines from letters are quoted as written; paraphrases are labelled.

beats.say: Christmas Eve, 1914. A bitter cold night, with white frost, on the Western Front in Belgium.

scene.date: Christmas Eve, a bitter cold night

beats.say: Soon after dusk, a shout comes across the frozen mud from the German trenches. Merry Christmas, Englishmen.

talk.text: Did they just say Merry Christmas?

beats.say: A British captain called Robert Miles will write it all down in a letter home. Men from both sides climb out, unarmed, and meet in no man's land. They swap cigarettes, he writes, and lies.

scene.caption: British and German troops in no man's land, Christmas 1914

beats.say: Somewhere along the same front, a German corporal in a Bavarian regiment does not approve at all. His name is Adolf Hitler.

scene.caption: Adolf Hitler (seated, right) with comrades of his regiment, 1914–1918

beats.say: About a hundred thousand British and German soldiers stop fighting that Christmas. Captain Miles writes that his men cannot shoot the Germans in cold blood. Five days later, he will be dead.
This is the Western Front, 1914 to 1918. Britain and France on one side, Germany on the other, and a line of trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland.
Today we live it from both sides of that line, minute by minute. And we ask one question. If the men in the trenches did not want to kill each other, why did the war go on for four more years?
August 1914. Germany sends seven armies west, and one east, against Russia. The plan in the west is to beat France fast, by going around the French defences, and then trapping the French army.
Going around means marching through Belgium, a neutral country. And Belgium's neutrality had been guaranteed by Britain, in a treaty signed in 1839.

talk.text: We go through Belgium. It is faster.

beats.say: On the fourth of August 1914, German armies attack Belgium. At midnight that same day, Britain's ultimatum runs out. Britain is at war.
The first battle is at Liège, a heavily fortified Belgian city. The siege lasts from the fifth to the sixteenth of August. Liège fights back so hard that it surprises the German army.

scene.caption: A fort at Liège after the siege, August 1914

beats.say: Brussels falls on the twentieth of August. On the twenty sixth, a British reservist called George Ellison lands in France with the 5th Royal Irish Lancers. He is thirty six years old.
His regiment's records say he fought near Mons that first summer. Remember the name of that town. George Ellison is going to come back to Mons.
Now the German side. The advance rolls on, south into France. Then, at the river Marne, it is halted.

scene.caption: French soldiers at the Marne, September 1914

talk.text: Nearly is a long way, it turns out.

beats.say: So both armies try to go around each other's northern end, again and again, all the way to the coast. It is called the Race to the Sea. Nobody wins it.
By late October 1914, there is one unbroken line of trenches, from the Swiss border to the North Sea. The war of movement is over. The war of digging has begun.
The first trenches are shallow ditches, crowded with men. Shellfire kills them in huge numbers. So both sides dig deeper. A good trench is at least two and a half metres deep.
Its walls are held up with sandbags, wire mesh and wood. On the floor lie wooden duckboards, over drainage channels, because the water always comes.

talk.text: Under the water. Same as yesterday.

beats.say: Now the other side of the line. German dugouts are built to last. They can be several storeys deep, at least four metres down, reinforced with concrete, with air vents.

A unit's turn in the front trench is usually short. Anything from a single day up to two weeks. Then it is relieved, and marches back. One Australian battalion once spent fifty three days in the line. That was a rare exception.

But the trench has enemies of its own. Trench foot comes from standing for days in cold, wet mud. It does not even need freezing weather. It starts with tingling and itching. Then numbness. Then sores.
And lice, in every seam of every uniform. Trench fever, spread by lice droppings, infects more than a million Allied soldiers.
Between the two front lines lies a strip of shell holes, wire and mud that belongs to nobody. The soldiers call it no man's land.
And in quiet parts of the front, something strange begins. Food comes up to the front line after dark. Soldiers on both sides notice that while they collect it, the other side does not shoot.
The lines are close enough to shout across. Many German soldiers had lived in England before the war, especially in London. Some shout over to ask for the football results.
Officers hate it. A young French lieutenant called Charles de Gaulle writes on the seventh of December about the lamentable wish of his men to leave the enemy in peace.
Christmas is coming. And on both sides, men are starting to wonder what they will do on the day.
Christmas Eve. The Germans put candles along their trenches, and on small Christmas trees. Then they begin to sing carols.
The British answer with carols of their own. Then come the greetings, shouted across the frozen ground.
Captain Robert Miles is with the Royal Irish Rifles. On Christmas Day he writes the letter that will make him remembered.

lines: A sort of unarranged and quite unauthorized
exists between us and our friends in front.

beats.say: Men from both sides leave their trenches, unarmed, and meet in what he calls the shot-riddled no man's land between the lines. They agree, all on their own, not to fire at each other until after midnight on Christmas Day.

talk.text: Are we allowed to do this?

beats.say: Across the line, a German lieutenant called Johannes Niemann grabs his binoculars. He looks over the parapet, and sees, he writes, the incredible sight of our soldiers exchanging cigarettes, schnapps and chocolate with the enemy.

lines: grabbed my binoculars and looking cautiously
over the parapet saw the incredible sight
schnapps and chocolate with the enemy

beats.say: Near Neuve Chapelle, a British general called Walter Congreve writes that one of his captains smoked a cigar with the best shot in the German army. The German marksman was no more than eighteen.
A nineteen year old private, Henry Williamson, writes to his mother on Boxing Day.
He writes. Dear Mother, I am writing from the trenches. In the pipe is German tobacco. From a German soldier. Yes a live German soldier from his own trench.

scene.header: Private Henry Williamson to his mother, 26 December 1914
lines: In the pipe is German tobacco.

beats.say: Burial parties go out, and the dead of both sides are brought in together. Joint services are held.

Captain Sir Edward Hulse, of the Scots Guards, meets a German interpreter who turns out to be from Suffolk. The man had left behind a girlfriend in England, and a three and a half horsepower motorcycle.

talk.text: I left a girl in Suffolk. And a motorcycle.
Which one do you miss more?

beats.say: Hulse writes that the sing-song ended with Auld Lang Syne, English, Scots, Irish, Prussians, all singing together. If I had seen it on a cinematograph film, he says, I should have sworn that it was faked.

lines: and if I had seen it on a cinematograph film
I should have sworn that it was faked!

beats.say: Another officer, Bruce Bairnsfather, takes a fancy to a German officer's buttons. He snips off two with his wire clippers, and gives the officer two of his own in exchange.
The last thing he sees is one of his machine gunners, a hairdresser before the war, cutting the long hair of a German who kneels patiently on the frozen ground.

talk.text: Not too short. I have a wife.

beats.say: Not every unit is at the front that day. Alfred Anderson, of the Black Watch, is in a farmhouse behind the lines. Eighty nine years later, as the last known surviving Scottish veteran of the war, he still remembers the silence. The eerie sound of silence.

And football? A Saxon lieutenant called Kurt Zehmisch wrote that the English brought a soccer ball from their trenches, and pretty soon a lively game ensued. How marvellously wonderful, he said, yet how strange it was.

lines: brought a soccer ball from their trenches,
and pretty soon a lively game ensued.

beats.say: Historians still argue about how many real matches there were. Some, it seems, were kick-abouts with a ration tin of bully beef for a ball.

It happens on the French line too. Gervais Morillon writes to his parents that the Germans waved a white flag, and came towards them unarmed. Then he adds, I am telling you this but don't speak of it to anyone.

lines: I am telling you this but
don't speak of it to anyone.

beats.say: Another Frenchman, Gustave Berthier, writes what the Germans told him. They were tired of making war. They were married, like me.
Boxing Day. In Captain Miles's sector, the truce simply carries on. He writes that the Germans ignore every warning to get down off their parapet.
And then come the words that sum up the whole of Christmas 1914. We can't shoot them in cold blood. I cannot see how we can get them to return to business.

lines: The beggars simply disregard all our warnings
to get down from off their parapet.
We can't shoot them in cold blood....
I cannot see how we can get them

beats.say: The generals can see exactly how. General Sir Horace Smith-Dorrien orders an end to friendly contact with the Germans.
On the German side, an order of the twenty ninth of December warns that every approach to the enemy will be punished as treason.

talk.text: The men are talking to the English, sir.
Then the men are committing treason.

beats.say: On the thirtieth of December 1914, Captain Robert Miles is killed in action. Five days after his Christmas letter.
In January, his letter is printed in the Daily Mail, and in his local paper in Shropshire. The readers meet a captain who would not shoot. By then, he is already gone.

lines: A CAPTAIN'S LETTER FROM THE FRONT
the truce, in his own words

beats.say: The truce is not reported for a week. The silence is broken on the thirty first of December by the New York Times, in neutral America. British papers follow. In France, the government reminds people that fraternising with the enemy is treason.
The next Christmas, in 1915, Allied commanders order raids and shelling all along the front, so that nothing like it happens again. It mostly doesn't.
In 1915, a Scots Guards company commander, Sir Iain Colquhoun, agrees a short truce to bury the dead. He is court-martialled for breaking standing orders, and found guilty.
Then General Douglas Haig cancels the punishment, and Colquhoun keeps his command. It may have helped that his wife's uncle was the Prime Minister, Herbert Asquith.

talk.text: Guilty of burying the dead, sir.

beats.say: So now we know the men will not always shoot. Which leaves the real question. Who will make them? The answer, in the spring of 1915, is a new weapon, that needs nobody to aim.
Spring 1915, near Ypres in Belgium. A German chemist called Fritz Haber has an idea. Chlorine gas. It is heavier than air, so it will stay low, close to the ground, where the trenches are.
German troops carry five thousand seven hundred and thirty gas cylinders into the front line. The biggest weigh forty kilograms each.

scene.date: carried into the line by hand

beats.say: Five thousand seven hundred and thirty cylinders, at up to forty kilograms each. That is up to two hundred and twenty nine tonnes, carried into the trenches by hand.

The gas cannot simply be opened, because the valves freeze. The liquid chlorine has to be siphoned out, to turn to vapour, and then the soldiers wait for the wind to carry it to the British and French lines.
On the twenty second of April 1915, the Second Battle of Ypres begins, with the first gas attack, launched from the German trench line near Langemark.
The weapon is dangerous to its owners too. Twice, shellfire breaks open German cylinders. The second time, three German soldiers are killed and fifty are wounded.
After Ypres, the French, the British and the Germans all use gas. In 1915 comes phosgene, which is more deadly. In 1917, mustard gas, which can linger for days.
Now every soldier on the front has two enemies he can see, and one he can't. And in 1916, both sides decide to win the war with one enormous battle each.
The twenty first of February 1916. The Germans attack the French fortress city of Verdun. It becomes a battle of three hundred and two days, one of the longest and costliest in human history.
Four days in, the Germans capture Fort Douaumont. Then the French commander, Philippe Pétain, orders that there be no retreat.

talk.text: No. We stay. Those are the orders.

beats.say: The French keep Verdun alive by road. About thirty four kilometres of road, six metres wide, are rebuilt and paved, just to carry the ammunition.
Now, the German side. In the German army at Verdun serves a man who, before the war, painted animals. Blue horses, red deer, a yellow cow. His name is Franz Marc.
He is one of the key figures of German Expressionism. In February 1916, he writes to his wife, Maria, that he has turned to camouflage.

He paints nine tarpaulin covers, to hide positions from aircraft, in styles, he says, from Manet to Kandinsky. He suspects the Kandinsky ones will work best against planes flying at two thousand metres or higher.

talk.text: Is that a painting or a gun?

beats.say: Meanwhile, the government has drawn up a list of notable artists, to be pulled out of the fighting for their own safety. Franz Marc's name is on that list.

scene.header: ~ 1916 ~ Notable artists to be withdrawn from combat (paraphrase)

beats.say: On the fourth of March 1916, near Verdun, a shell splinter strikes him in the head. He is killed instantly. The orders to move him to safety have not reached him yet. He is thirty six.

Years earlier, he had written on the back of one of his paintings: And all being is flaming agony. During the war, he told his wife that painting was like a premonition of this war. Horrible and shattering.

scene.header: Franz Marc, on the back of a canvas
lines: Und Alles Sein ist flammend Leid
And all being is flaming agony

beats.say: Remember the corporal who opposed the Christmas truce. Twenty three years later, his government sold Franz Marc's Blue Horses at a sale of what it called degenerate art.

Verdun goes on until December. By one modern count, the French lose three hundred and seventy seven thousand men killed, wounded or missing, and the Germans three hundred and thirty seven thousand. About seventy thousand a month.

card.note: Heer and Naumann (2000), via Battle of Verdun

beats.say: That summer, Britain attacks further north, on the river Somme, with five French divisions on its right. And under the German front line, British tunnellers have placed nineteen mines.
The largest, at La Boisselle, hold twenty four tons of explosive each. One of them is called Lochnagar.
For eight days, British guns pound the German line. The shells are meant to cut the wire and smash the defences, before the infantry cross no man's land.
Now, the other side of that bombardment. The German soldiers are deep underground, in dugouts that the shells cannot reach. They wait. They listen.

talk.text: When it stops, we go up.

beats.say: The first of July 1916. At seven twenty, the Hawthorn Ridge mine is blown. At seven twenty eight, the others. At seven thirty, the whistles blow, and the British infantry go over the top.

scene.caption: Royal Irish Rifles before going over the top, 1 July 1916

beats.say: The bombardment has not cut the German wire, and it has not destroyed the deep dugouts. The German machine gunners climb out, and they are ready.
By the end of that day, the British have suffered fifty seven thousand four hundred and seventy casualties. Nineteen thousand two hundred and forty of them are dead.
Nineteen thousand two hundred and forty dead, in one day. If you spread them over all twenty four hours, that is about eight hundred every hour.
In places, the two sides agree small truces, so the wounded can be carried in from no man's land. Even on that day, the men find a way.
The Battle of the Somme goes on for months, with over a million casualties on both sides. And the men who survive it carry something home that nobody yet knows how to name.
Soldiers call it shell shock. The symptoms are a fixed stare, shaking, being unable to speak, ringing in the ears.

card.sub: a term born in the First World War

beats.say: Doctors at the time barely know what it is. Men who do not get better are sent back to special centres behind the lines, labelled N Y D N. Not yet diagnosed, nervous.

talk.text: That's all right. Take your time.

beats.say: Now the French side. In 1917, whole French units refuse to attack. Mutinies break out in fifty four French divisions. Twenty thousand men desert.

talk.text: But we will not attack. Not again.

beats.say: And on the sixth of April 1917, the United States declares war on Germany. A new army will cross the Atlantic. The question is whether it will arrive in time.
Among the Americans drafted that September is a bank clerk from Baltimore called Henry Gunther. His family is German American. Keep him in mind.

Meanwhile, in Flanders, the British attack again, at Passchendaele, over low fields cut by streams and ditches. An unusually wet August, then the autumn rains, turn it to mud. The cost is put at four hundred and eighty seven thousand casualties.
Now the German side. The German commanders decide that their only remaining chance is to beat the Allies before the Americans can cross the Atlantic in strength.

The twenty first of March 1918. Germany launches its spring offensive. The Germans call it the Kaiser's Battle. Their aim is to beat the Allies before the United States can bring its full strength across the Atlantic.

talk.text: We have one spring to win this war.

beats.say: German armies gain ground along whole sections of the front. The line moves again. But supplies still come by railway and by horse, and horse-drawn transport cannot keep up with a deep advance.
By July, the offensive is finished. The casualties run to the hundreds of thousands on each side. And now it is the Allies' turn.
Henry Gunther arrives in France in July 1918, as a supply sergeant. He writes home about the miserable conditions at the front, and tells a friend to try anything to avoid being drafted.

lines: Try anything to avoid being drafted.

beats.say: The army censor opens that letter. Gunther is demoted from sergeant to private.

talk.text: Then he can be a miserable private.

beats.say: Through the late summer and autumn, the Allied advance does not stop. It is called the Hundred Days Offensive. The German armies begin to collapse, and their commanders decide that defeat cannot be avoided.

At home, Germany is starving under the Allied blockade. On the ninth of November, the chancellor hands over power to Friedrich Ebert. And a German delegation is on its way to France, to ask for an armistice.

The morning of the eighth of November. After ten hours driving across the wrecked north of France, the German delegation reaches a railway siding in the Forest of Compiègne. Waiting there is the private train of the French marshal, Ferdinand Foch.

scene.caption: Foch's railway carriage, Forest of Compiègne, 1918

beats.say: The Germans are handed the Allied terms, and given seventy two hours to agree. They ask for an immediate ceasefire, to stop the killing while they talk. Foch refuses.

talk.text: Stop the fighting while we talk.
No. Sign, and then it stops.

beats.say: Five o'clock in the morning, on the eleventh of November 1918. The armistice is agreed in Foch's carriage. It will take effect at eleven o'clock. Six more hours of war.
All along the front, many artillery units keep firing, rather than haul their spare shells away. Commanders want the best possible position, in case the fighting starts again.
Nine thirty. On the edge of Mons, in Belgium, a British private on patrol in a wood is shot by a sniper. His name is George Ellison. He fought near Mons in 1914. Four years later, he dies there.

Near the river Meuse, a French messenger called Augustin Trébuchon is carrying a note to the troops. It says soup will be served at half past eleven, after the peace. He is forty, a shepherd, and he played the accordion at village weddings.

That morning, his division has been ordered across the flooded Meuse, seventy metres wide, in freezing rain. Engineers build a plank footbridge in the dark. A little after eight, about seven hundred men cross. Some fall in, and drown.
At ten forty five, he is shot. Fifteen minutes before the end. Later, embarrassed, the French army writes the date of his death down as the day before.
Ten fifty eight. A Canadian private, George Price, is killed by a sniper near Mons. Two minutes before the armistice.

Ten fifty nine. In the village of Chaumont-devant-Damvillers, Henry Gunther's squad comes up against two German machine guns. Against his sergeant's orders, Gunther gets up and charges, with his rifle.
The German gunners know the war will end in one minute. They try to wave him away. He keeps coming. He is hit, and dies instantly. He is twenty three.
Eleven o'clock. The guns stop.
On that last day alone, there were ten thousand nine hundred and forty four casualties. Two thousand seven hundred and thirty eight men died. More than on most ordinary days of the war.
The next day, the American commander, General Pershing, names Henry Gunther as the last American killed in the war. The army gives him back his rank of sergeant.

scene.header: General Pershing, Order of the Day, 12 November 1918 (paraphrase)

beats.say: The Western Front lasted one thousand five hundred and sixty days, from the fourth of August 1914 to the eleventh of November 1918.
On the Allied side, about two million and forty one thousand soldiers died. On the German side, about one million four hundred and ninety five thousand.
Put together, that is about two thousand two hundred and seventy soldiers dead, every single day, for one thousand five hundred and sixty days.
So which side was right? The British and French would say they were defending Belgium, and France, from an invasion. That is true.
And the Germans who talked to Gustave Berthier at Christmas said they had no quarrel with the French. They were married. They were tired of making war.

But look at what the men on both sides kept doing, whenever they were left alone. They held their fire while the food came up. They sang to each other. They traded tobacco and buttons, and buried each other's dead.

It took orders, threats of treason, new weapons and enormous battles to keep them fighting. Captain Robert Miles had wondered how anyone could get them to return to business. Now we know. The business ran for about fourteen hundred more days.

And the corporal who opposed the truce? Twenty two years later, he had Foch's railway carriage moved back to its exact spot in the forest, for France to sign an armistice with him. That is another border, and another story.

card.sub: the same carriage, the same clearing

beats.say: One German soldier from that time could not stop thinking about it. Richard Schirrmann saw French and German troops make their own peace in the Vosges mountains, at Christmas 1915. He wondered if young people of all countries could be given places to meet, and get to know each other.
In 1919, he founded the German Youth Hostel Association. Cheap beds, under one roof, for strangers from anywhere. A soldier's idea from a Christmas in the trenches.
Two lines of trenches. A strip of mud between them that belonged to nobody. And on Christmas Day, for a few hours, it belonged to everybody.

outro.text: Every border has two sides. On the Western Front, the two sides were often closer to each other than to the men who gave the orders.
outro.question: If you had been in the trench that Christmas, would you have climbed out?

de.title: Wie die Westfront geschah — Minute für Minute
de.description:
Heiligabend 1914: Deutsche Soldaten rufen „Merry Christmas“ über das Niemandsland, und ein britischer Hauptmann schreibt, seine Männer könnten sie nicht kaltblütig erschießen. Fünf Tage später ist er tot.

Die Westfront 1914–1918, erlebt von beiden Seiten der Schützengräben: der Marsch durch Belgien, das Leben zweieinhalb Meter unter der Erde, der Weihnachtsfrieden in den Briefen von Robert Miles, Johannes Niemann und Kurt Zehmisch, das erste Gas bei Ypern, der Maler Franz Marc vor Verdun, 7:30 Uhr am ersten Tag an der Somme und die letzten Minuten des 11. November 1918.

es.title: Cómo ocurrió el Frente Occidental — Minuto a minuto
es.description:
Nochebuena de 1914: los alemanes gritan «Merry Christmas» a través de la tierra de nadie, y un capitán británico escribe que sus hombres no pueden dispararles a sangre fría. Cinco días después, está muerto.

El Frente Occidental de 1914 a 1918, vivido desde los dos lados de las trincheras: la marcha por Bélgica, la vida bajo tierra, la tregua de Navidad en las cartas de soldados de ambos bandos, el primer ataque con gas en Ypres, el pintor Franz Marc en Verdún, las 7:30 del primer día del Somme y los últimos minutos del 11 de noviembre de 1918.

fr.title: Comment le front de l'Ouest est arrivé — minute par minute
fr.description:
Veillée de Noël 1914 : les Allemands crient « Merry Christmas » à travers le no man's land, et un capitaine britannique écrit que ses hommes ne peuvent pas les abattre de sang-froid. Cinq jours plus tard, il est mort.

Le front de l'Ouest de 1914 à 1918, vécu des deux côtés des tranchées : la marche à travers la Belgique, la vie sous terre, la trêve de Noël dans les lettres de soldats britanniques, allemands et français, le premier gaz à Ypres, le peintre Franz Marc à Verdun, 7 h 30 le premier jour de la Somme, et les dernières minutes du 11 novembre 1918, jusqu'à Augustin Trébuchon.

pt.title: Como aconteceu a Frente Ocidental — Minuto a minuto
pt.description:
Véspera de Natal de 1914: os alemães gritam «Merry Christmas» pela terra de ninguém, e um capitão britânico escreve que seus homens não conseguem atirar neles a sangue-frio. Cinco dias depois, ele está morto.

A Frente Ocidental de 1914 a 1918, vivida dos dois lados das trincheiras: a marcha pela Bélgica, a vida debaixo da terra, a trégua de Natal nas cartas de soldados dos dois lados, o primeiro ataque com gás em Ypres, o pintor Franz Marc em Verdun, as 7h30 do primeiro dia do Somme e os últimos minutos de 11 de novembro de 1918.
